analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks on all firearm sales at gun shows.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every firearm sale at a gun show to go through a licensed dealer, who would run a criminal background check on the buyer and keep records. It would also require gun show organizers to register with the Justice Department, tell it in advance who will be selling, and let federal agents inspect show records. The bill was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never advanced out of committee before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk from guns sold without background checks. Federal research and the bill's own findings say gun shows are a place where prohibited buyers — people with felony convictions, domestic violence records, or other disqualifiers — can buy firearms from private sellers with no check and no paper trail [S3]. Requiring a dealer-run background check on those sales would close that channel, the same way sales at licensed stores already work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Buyers and communities affected by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Requires a licensed dealer to facilitate every private firearm transfer at a gun show and run the federal background check system on the buyer, making gun show sales match the rules already in place at gun stores.

Requires gun show operators to register with the Attorney General, provide fingerprints and photos, notify the government of each vendor 30 days before the show, and keep vendor records — so unlicensed sellers are identified rather than anonymous.

Lets the Justice Department inspect gun show records without a warrant during business hours, directs ATF to hire at least 40 additional investigators for gun show inspections, and raises penalties for background-check violations from 1 year to 5 years in prison.
Requires biennial ATF reports to Congress on whether firearms are being sold at gun shows without background checks.

analysis.who_pays: Unlicensed private sellers at gun shows, who could no longer sell to strangers without going through a licensed dealer; gun show operators, who face registration fees, paperwork, and federal inspection; and licensed dealers, who take on new recordkeeping and reporting work for these facilitated transfers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun show operators and private sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill adds significant compliance costs: operators must register and pay fees, keep vendor ledgers, and submit to warrantless inspections, and the bill directs at least 40 new federal investigators — costs that small shows and individual collectors argue fall heavily on hobbyists and small-time sellers, not criminals.

The definition of a regulated gun show is narrow — it excludes private collection sales at a home and small, members-only hunting-club events — so sellers could shift to venues just outside the rules rather than buying and selling legally through the new process.
A background check takes time and money, which supporters of the current rules argue discourages casual, legal sales between neighbors at shows without stopping determined illegal buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: closing the only large, organized venue where firearms routinely change hands with no background check and no records. The costs are compliance burdens on private sellers, show operators, and dealers, and the bill is drawn tightly enough (small shows, private collections, members-only club events are excluded) that determined sellers can avoid it. It would not stop most gun crime on its own, but it extends to gun shows the same check that already applies at gun stores.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on May 5, 2023.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.
Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private sellers at gun shows and gun show operators keep the current rules, where private sales can happen without background checks or records; anyone who prefers to buy that way is unaffected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unregulated private sellers at gun shows

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress, letting it expire.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes, so there is no record of how members of either party would have voted.

industries.note: They would face federal registration with fingerprints and photos, pre-show vendor reporting, recordkeeping, and warrantless inspections. Their interest in avoiding these requirements runs against the bill's purpose of tracing gun show sales.

Every private transfer at a gun show would have to be facilitated by a licensed dealer, creating a stream of fee-paying background-check business for them. Dealers also take on new reporting duties and higher penalties for recordkeeping violations.
They could no longer sell to strangers at shows without a dealer-run background check and a record of the sale. Selling without the check would carry criminal penalties of up to 5 years.

Manufacturers sell little directly at gun shows, and the bill barely touches them, but tighter checks at shows can reduce the secondary market that competes with new-gun sales while raising enforcement scrutiny across licensed channels.
